title: Interference-Aware Edge Runtime Prediction with Conformal Matrix Completion
problem: Predicting workload runtime on heterogeneous edge computing platforms under multi-tenant interference, where observation data is sparse and platforms vary widely in architecture.
motivation: Edge deployments span diverse hardware (ARM, x86, RISC-V, microcontrollers) and are often shared among workloads; sparse runtime observations make traditional regression or single-platform models insufficient for accurate cross-platform, cross-workload prediction under contention.
method: Pitot uses a pair of neural networks that together apply matrix factorization—a technique for estimating missing values by decomposing data—to predict runtime. The networks take two types of information as input: features describing the workload's instructions (opcode counts) and specifications of the hardware platform. The system adds a low-rank bilinear interference term (a compact mathematical component modeling how multiple simultaneous workloads slow each other by competing for resources) directly into the learned representation. It's trained by minimizing log-scale prediction errors and provides confidence intervals via conformalized quantile regression with optimal quantile selection, calibrated separately for each platform type.
key_novelty: Pitot integrates the interference model—the mathematical component capturing how concurrent workloads slow each other—directly into the matrix factorization embedding space via a low-rank bilinear term, enabling joint estimation of missing runtime values and interference effects from sparse observations.
contributions: Two-tower MLP matrix factorization with opcode-count and platform side information for cross-platform runtime prediction
Low-rank bilinear interference term in embedding space for multi-tenant contention modeling
Conformalized quantile regression with optimal quantile selection and per-platform calibration pools for coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals
Evaluation on CNN vision benchmarks and HPC Polybench suite across diverse edge platforms

metrics.accuracy: 5.2% MAPE; up to 48% lower error and 44% tighter prediction intervals vs next-best baseline
metrics.other: 2x improvement over naive matrix factorization baseline

limitations: Requires opcode-count feature extraction from workloads (binary instrumentation)
Calibration pool must be populated per platform before deployment
Assumes interference effect is low-rank in embedding space
